en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on False Speech 1.
The Training Rule on False Speech.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Now, venerable friends, these ninety-two *pācittiya* rules come up for recitation.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, Hatthaka the Sakyan was a champion debater.

Thus, while conversing with the wanderers, Hatthaka the Sakyan son denies what he has admitted, admits what he has denied, evades the issue with prevarication, speaks deliberate falsehoods, and deceives them by making secret agreements.

The wanderers were indignant, disparaged him, and complained, saying: "How can it be that Hatthaka the Sakyan son, while conversing with us, denies what he has admitted, admits what he has denied, and evades the issue with prevarication?"
“He will pursue her, he will speak a deliberate lie, and having made an appointment, he will deceive her.
The bhikkhus heard those sectarians criticizing, disparaging, and complaining in this way.
Then those bhikkhus approached Hatthaka of the Sakyans; having approached, they said this to Hatthaka of the Sakyans:
“Is it true, friend Hatthaka, that while conversing with the followers of other sects, you admitted what you had denied, denied what you had admitted,
evaded one question with another, spoke deliberate falsehoods, and deceived them by making a secret agreement? “Indeed, friend,
those who are called ‘followers of other sects’ can be defeated by any means whatsoever.”
“Victory should not be granted to them.
Those monks who were few in desires... [as above] ...were indignant, disparaged [this], and complained:
“How can Hatthaka of the Sakyans, while conversing with the followers of other sects, claim to have understood what he has actually failed to understand?”
“Having made a claim, he will deny it; he will evade one question with another; he will speak deliberate falsehoods;
having made an appointment, he will deceive.
Then those bhikkhus, having rebuked Hatthaka the Sakyan in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this context, having assembled the community of monks, questioned Hatthaka the Sakyan:
“Is it true, Hatthaka, that while conversing with the followers of other sects, you admitted what you had denied and denied what you had admitted;
that you evaded the issue with one thing or another, spoke a deliberate lie, and broke your word after making an agreement?”
“It is true, Blessed One,” he replied.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, while conversing with those of other sects, deny something and then later claim it?”
Having admitted it, you will deny it; you will evade one question with another; you will speak a deliberate lie;
having made an appointment, you will deceive.
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so forth].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
"In the case of a deliberate lie, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Now, what is called a deliberate lie?
The speech, the utterance, the expression, the vocal articulation, the vocal intimation, and the eight ignoble modes of speech of one who intends to deceive:
"What was not seen, I have seen"; "what was not heard, I have heard"; "what was not sensed, I have sensed"; "what was not cognized, I have cognized";
"what was seen, I have not seen"; "what was heard, I have not heard"; "what was sensed, I have not sensed"; "what was cognized, I have not cognized."
"Unseen" means not seen by the eye.
"Unheard" means...
Not heard with the ear.
That which is called "unperceived" is not smelled by the nose, not tasted by the tongue, and not touched by the body.
The "unknown" means not cognized by the mind.
The "seen" means...
"Seen" means seen with the eye.
"Hear" means heard with the ear.
The cognized (muta) is that which is smelled by the nose, tasted by the tongue, and touched by the body.
The known (viññāta) is...
“Known by the mind.
In three ways, for one who speaks a deliberate lie, saying “I have seen what was not seen,” there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya):
previously he thinks, “I will speak a lie”; while speaking he thinks, “I am speaking a lie”; having spoken he thinks, “A lie has been spoken by me.”
In four ways, for one who speaks a deliberate lie, saying “I have seen what I have not seen,” there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya):
previously he thinks, “I will speak a lie”; while speaking he thinks, “I am speaking a lie”; having spoken he thinks, “A lie has been spoken by me”; and he conceals his view.
In five ways, for one who speaks a deliberate lie, saying “I have seen what I have not seen,” there is an offense of expiation.

There is the case where, before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak falsely"; while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking falsely"; and after having spoken, one thinks, "I have spoken falsely," having set aside one's view, having set aside one's preference.
There is an offense of expiation for one who speaks a deliberate lie, saying "I have seen what I have not seen," in six ways:

before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak falsely"; while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking falsely"; after having spoken, one thinks, "I have spoken falsely," having set aside one's view, having set aside one's preference, and having set aside one's inclination.
In seven ways, for one who speaks a deliberate lie, saying "I have seen what was not seen," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya):
namely, when he has the thought beforehand, "I will speak a lie"; while speaking, he has the thought, "I am speaking a lie";

and having spoken, he has the thought, "A lie has been spoken by me"—this being done by misrepresenting his view, misrepresenting his preference, misrepresenting his inclination, and misrepresenting his disposition.
In three ways, for one who speaks a deliberate lie, saying "I have heard what I have not heard," ...pe...
"I have sensed what I have not sensed," ...pe...
"I have cognized what I have not cognized," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Previously, one thinks: "I will speak falsely"; while speaking, one thinks: "I am speaking falsely"; having spoken, one thinks: "Falsehood has been spoken by me. In four ways...
[as above] ...in five ways... [as above].
In six ways … [and] in seven ways, for one who speaks a deliberate lie, thinking “what is unknown to me is known to me,” there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya):
previously he thinks, “I will speak a lie”; while speaking, he thinks, “I am speaking a lie”; having spoken, [he knows it].
It occurs [to one] who thinks, "I have spoken falsely," having set aside his view, having set aside his inclination, having set aside his preference, and having set aside his disposition.
For one who speaks a deliberate lie in three ways, saying, "What was not seen has been seen by me, and what was heard has been heard by me," there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)...
For one who speaks a deliberate lie in three ways, saying, "What was not seen has been seen by me, and what was sensed has been sensed by me," there is an offense of expiation...

In three ways, for one who speaks a deliberate lie, saying of what has not been seen: “It has been seen and it has been cognized by me,” there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) … [and so on] … In three ways, of what has not been seen:
“It has been seen, heard, and sensed by me” … [and so on] … In three ways, of what has not been seen: “It has been seen, heard, and cognized by me” … [and so on] …

If one speaks a deliberate lie in three ways, saying of what has not been seen: “I have seen it, and I have heard it, and I have sensed it, and I have cognized it,” there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) …pe…. If one speaks a deliberate lie in three ways, saying of what has not been heard:
“I have heard it, and I have sensed it,” …pe… If one speaks a deliberate lie in three ways, saying of what has not been heard: “I have heard it, and I have cognized it,” …pe…

If one intentionally speaks a falsehood, saying of what has not been heard, “I have heard it and I have seen it,” there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). … [and so on] … If one intentionally speaks a falsehood, saying of what has not been heard,
“I have heard it and I have sensed it and I have cognized it,” … [and so on] … If one intentionally speaks a falsehood,
saying of what has not been heard, “I have heard it and I have sensed it and I have seen it,” … [and so on] …
If one consciously speaks a falsehood, saying "I have heard, sensed, cognized, and seen" regarding what has not been heard, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)...
[and so on] ...if one consciously speaks a falsehood, saying "I have sensed and cognized" regarding what has not been sensed...
[and so on] ...if one consciously speaks a falsehood, saying "I have sensed and seen" regarding what has not been sensed... [and so on].
If one consciously speaks a falsehood regarding what has not been personally experienced, saying, “I have experienced it, and I have heard it,” there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

… [and so on] … If one consciously speaks a falsehood regarding what has not been personally experienced, saying, “I have experienced it, and I have cognized it, and I have seen it,” … [and so on] … If one consciously speaks a falsehood regarding what has not been personally experienced, saying, “I have experienced it, and I have cognized it, and I have heard it,” … [and so on] …

If one speaks a deliberate lie with three modes, saying of what has not been sensed: "It has been sensed by me, and it has been cognized, seen, and heard," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

… [and so on] … If one speaks with three modes of what has not been cognized: "It has been cognized by me, and it has been seen," … [and so on] … If one speaks with three modes of what has not been cognized: "It has been cognized by me, and it has been heard," … [and so on] …
If one consciously speaks a falsehood, saying "I have known and sensed it" regarding what has not been known in three ways, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)...
[and so on] ...if one consciously speaks a falsehood, saying "I have known and seen and heard it" regarding what has not been known in three ways...
[and so on] ...if one consciously speaks a falsehood, saying "I have known and seen and sensed it" regarding what has not been known in three ways... [and so on].
If one speaks a conscious lie in three ways, saying of what is unknown: "It is known by me, seen, heard, and sensed," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
…pe… In three ways, [saying] of what is seen: "It is not seen by me" …pe… of what is heard:
"It is not heard by me" …pe…

If one speaks a deliberate lie, saying of what has been sensed, "It has not been sensed by me" ... pe ... or of what has been cognized, "It has not been cognized by me," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) ... pe ...
In three ways, if one says of what has been seen, "I have heard it" ... pe ...
If one speaks a deliberate lie, saying of what was seen through three modes,

“It was heard by me,” … [and so on] … if one speaks a deliberate lie, saying of what was seen through three modes, “It was cognized by me,” there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). … [and so on] … if one speaks a deliberate lie, saying of what was seen through three modes,
“It was both heard and sensed by me,” … [and so on] …
If one speaks a deliberate lie, saying of what was seen: "It has been heard by me and it has been cognized by me," ...

[as before] ... if one speaks a deliberate lie, saying of what was seen: "It has been heard by me and it has been sensed by me and it has been cognized by me," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
... [as before] ... If one speaks a deliberate lie, saying of what was heard: "It has been sensed by me," ... [as before] ...
If one speaks a conscious lie, saying of what was heard through three modes,

“It was cognized by me,” … [as before] … if one speaks a conscious lie, saying of what was heard through three modes, “It was seen by me,” there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) … [as before] … if one speaks a conscious lie,
saying of what was heard through three modes, “It was sensed and cognized by me,” … [as before] …
If one speaks a conscious lie, saying of what was heard through three modes,

“It was smelt by me and seen by me,” … [as before] … if one speaks a conscious lie, saying of what was heard through three modes, “It was smelt by me, cognized by me, and seen by me,” there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
… [as before] … If one speaks of what was smelt through three modes, “It was cognized by me,” … [as before] …
If one speaks a conscious lie, saying of what was sensed through three modes, "I have seen it," ...
[and so on] ... if one speaks a conscious lie, saying of what was sensed through three modes, "I have heard it," there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) ... [and so on] ...
if one speaks a conscious lie, saying of what was sensed through three modes, "It was both sensed by me and seen by me," ... [and so on] ...
If one says of what has been sensed through three modes,

"It was cognized by me and heard by me" … [as before] … if one speaks a conscious lie, saying of what has been sensed through three modes, "It was cognized by me, seen by me, and heard by me," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) … [as before] … If one says of what has been cognized through three modes, "It was seen by me" … [as before] …
If one knowingly speaks falsely, saying of what is cognized through three modes, "I have heard it," ...
[and so on] ... if one knowingly speaks falsely, saying of what is cognized through three modes, "I have sensed it," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). ... [and so on] ...
if one knowingly speaks falsely, saying of what is cognized through three modes, "I have both seen and heard it," ... [and so on] ...
If one consciously speaks falsehood, saying of what is known through three modes, "I have seen it and I have sensed it," ...

[and so on] ... if one consciously speaks falsehood, saying of what is known through three modes, "I have seen it, heard it, and sensed it," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). ... [And so on] ...
When one is doubtful regarding what was seen through three modes, one does not accept it as seen, one does not remember it as seen, or one has forgotten it as seen. ... [And so on] ...
Being doubtful about what has been heard, one does not accept what has been heard; one forgets what has been heard; one becomes confused regarding what has been heard.
… Being doubtful about what has been sensed, one does not accept what has been sensed; one forgets what has been sensed; one becomes confused regarding what has been sensed.

… Being doubtful about what has been cognized, one does not accept what has been cognized; one forgets what has been cognized; one becomes confused regarding what has been cognized. … “What has been cognized by me and seen by me” … [and so on].
He forgets what he has cognized... "What I have cognized and heard"—[and so on]...
he forgets what he has cognized; "What I have cognized and sensed"—[and so on]...
he forgets what he has cognized; "What I have cognized, seen, and heard"—[and so on]...
He forgets what was cognized; "What was cognized by me, seen, heard, and sensed... [and so on] ...he forgets what was cognized;
"What was cognized by me, seen, heard, sensed, and known"—for one who speaks such a deliberate lie, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
In four ways... [and so on].

In five ways … [and so on] … in six ways … [and so on] … in seven ways … if one forgets what was cognized and speaks a deliberate lie, saying, "I have cognized, and I have seen, heard, sensed, and known," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
There is no offense if, before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak falsely"; while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking falsely";
and after having spoken, one thinks, "I have spoken falsely," having set aside one's view, set aside one's conviction, set aside one's preference, and set aside one's disposition.
There is no offense.
She speaks with a laugh;
she speaks with a cry.
"To speak with a laugh" means:
He speaks impulsively.
What is called "speaking abruptly" is when one says something else than what one intended to say.
"In the case of one who is insane,
and in the case of the first offender.
The first training rule on false speech is concluded.
